questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the main risk of rolling out a full governance program company-wide right after getting budget approval?
options: It scales whatever mistakes are baked into the first attempt right along with it, before they've been caught
It takes longer than a pilot to get executive approval
It is less expensive than a scoped pilot
It eliminates the need for a business case entirely
questions.explain: Scaling too fast scales the mistakes too — a confusing RACI, an unrealistic policy, or an unadopted tool spreads across the whole organization instead of staying contained to one small pilot.

questions.q: What are the three criteria for choosing a good pilot domain?
options: High value, high pain, and high feasibility
Low cost, low risk, and low visibility
High complexity, high headcount, and high regulatory exposure
Executive preference, vendor availability, and tooling maturity
questions.explain: The best pilot domain scores well on all three: it matters to the business (value), people already feel the problem (pain), and a small team can actually finish within a defined window (feasibility).

questions.q: Why is a baseline measurement necessary before a pilot begins?
options: Without it, there is nothing to compare the end-of-pilot result against, so a scale-or-stop decision can't be made on real evidence
It is required by regulation before any pilot can launch
It replaces the need for a named owner
It determines how long the pilot's time window should be
questions.explain: "It feels better now" doesn't survive a scale-or-stop decision — the baseline is what makes the end-of-pilot result meaningful.

questions.q: A pilot domain that is high-value and high-pain but spans twelve systems and four business units has what problem?
options: It fails the feasibility criterion — it's a program, not a pilot
It fails the value criterion because too many people care about it
It fails the pain criterion because the problem is too visible
It has no problem — more systems make a pilot stronger
questions.explain: A domain that's too large or complex to finish within a defined window fails feasibility — this is the most common way 'starting small' quietly becomes 'starting the same big thing, just called a pilot.'

questions.q: What happens at a pilot's 'scale-or-stop decision point'?
options: The team compares the baseline against the result and explicitly decides to scale, adjust, or stop the effort
The executive sponsor is replaced with a new one
The pilot's time window is extended indefinitely by default
A new business case is written from scratch regardless of the outcome
questions.explain: The scale-or-stop decision is a planned moment at the end of the fixed time window where the baseline-vs-result numbers drive an explicit decision, rather than letting the pilot drift on indefinitely.
